question: What is normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF briefly.
key_points: organising tables to reduce redundancy and update/insert/delete anomalies
1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
2NF: 1NF plus no partial dependency on part of a composite key
3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency of non-key attributes

question: What are ACID properties of a transaction?
key_points: Atomicity: all or nothing
Consistency: moves the database from one valid state to another
Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere
Durability: committed changes survive crashes

question: What is an index in a database and when should you not use one?
key_points: data structure (often B+ tree) that speeds up lookups
avoids full table scans
costs extra storage and slows inserts/updates
not worth it on small tables or columns with few distinct values or write-heavy tables

question: Explain the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN with an example.
key_points: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables
LEFT JOIN returns all rows of the left table
unmatched right side columns become NULL
a concrete example such as students and marks

question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
key_points: process is a program in execution with its own address space
threads share the process memory and resources
threads are lighter to create and switch
a crash or bug in one thread can affect the whole process

question: What is a deadlock? State the necessary conditions.
key_points: processes wait forever for resources held by each other
mutual exclusion
hold and wait
no preemption
circular wait

question: What is paging and why is it used?
key_points: memory split into fixed-size pages and frames
page table maps logical pages to physical frames
removes external fragmentation
allows non-contiguous allocation and virtual memory

question: What is the difference between a mutex and a semaphore?
key_points: mutex allows one thread into a critical section and has an owner
semaphore is a counter allowing up to N
binary semaphore vs counting semaphore
semaphores can be signalled by a different thread than the one that waited

question: Compare TCP and UDP. When would you use UDP?
key_points: TCP is connection-oriented with a handshake
TCP guarantees ordered, reliable delivery with retransmission and flow/congestion control
UDP is connectionless with no delivery guarantee and lower overhead
UDP suits video calls, gaming, DNS, live streaming

question: What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?
key_points: DNS resolves the domain to an IP address
TCP connection and TLS handshake for HTTPS
browser sends an HTTP request and the server returns a response
browser parses HTML and loads CSS/JS/images and renders the page

question: Name the layers of the OSI model and one protocol at any three of them.
key_points: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application
network layer example: IP
transport layer example: TCP or UDP
application layer example: HTTP, DNS, FTP

question: Explain the four pillars of object-oriented programming.
key_points: encapsulation: bundling data and methods, hiding internal state
abstraction: exposing only essential behaviour
inheritance: a class reuses and extends another
polymorphism: one interface, many implementations (overloading/overriding)

question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
key_points: overloading: same name, different parameters, in the same class
resolved at compile time
overriding: subclass redefines a parent method with the same signature
resolved at runtime (dynamic dispatch)

question: When would you use an interface instead of an abstract class?
key_points: interface defines a contract with no state
a class can implement many interfaces but extend one class
abstract class can hold shared state and partial implementation
use interface for capabilities across unrelated classes

question: Compare arrays and linked lists. When would you choose a linked list?
key_points: array has O(1) random access and contiguous memory
linked list insertion/deletion at a known node is O(1)
linked list access is O(n) and has pointer overhead
choose linked list for frequent inserts/deletes and unknown size

question: How does a hash map work internally?
key_points: hash function maps a key to a bucket index
average O(1) insert and lookup
collisions handled by chaining or open addressing
resizing/rehashing when the load factor grows

question: What is the time complexity of quicksort and merge sort, and which would you pick?
key_points: merge sort O(n log n) in all cases, needs O(n) extra space, stable
quicksort O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst case
quicksort is in-place and usually faster in practice
pick merge sort when stability or guaranteed worst case matters, e.g. linked lists

question: What is the difference between a stack and a queue? Give a real use of each.
key_points: stack is LIFO
queue is FIFO
stack use: function call stack, undo, bracket matching
queue use: scheduling, BFS, printer or request queues

question: Explain BFS and DFS. When is BFS better?
key_points: BFS explores level by level using a queue
DFS goes deep first using a stack or recursion
BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph
both are O(V + E)

question: What is overfitting and how do you prevent it?
key_points: model fits training noise and performs poorly on unseen data
detected by a gap between training and validation performance
fixes: more data, regularization (L1/L2, dropout), simpler model
early stopping, cross-validation, data augmentation

question: Explain the bias-variance trade-off.
key_points: bias: error from overly simple assumptions, causes underfitting
variance: sensitivity to training data, causes overfitting
increasing model complexity lowers bias but raises variance
goal is the complexity that minimises total error on unseen data

question: What are precision and recall? When is recall more important?
key_points: precision = TP / (TP + FP): of predicted positives, how many are right
recall = TP / (TP + FN): of actual positives, how many were found
trade-off controlled by the decision threshold; F1 combines them
recall matters when missing a positive is costly, e.g. disease or fraud detection

question: Why do we split data into train, validation and test sets?
key_points: train set fits the model parameters
validation set tunes hyperparameters and picks the model
test set is used once for an unbiased final estimate
tuning on the test set leaks information and inflates the score

question: How does gradient descent work? What does the learning rate do?
key_points: iteratively updates parameters in the direction of the negative gradient of the loss
learning rate sets the step size
too high diverges or oscillates, too low is slow or stuck
variants: stochastic / mini-batch, momentum, Adam

question: Why do CNNs work well for images?
key_points: convolution filters detect local patterns such as edges and textures
weight sharing means far fewer parameters than a fully connected network
pooling / stride give some translation invariance
stacked layers build a hierarchy from edges to shapes to objects

question: What is attention in transformers, in simple words?
key_points: each token builds its representation by weighting all other tokens
weights come from query-key similarity (softmax of scaled dot products)
captures long-range dependencies without recurrence
runs in parallel across the sequence; multi-head attention looks at different relations

question: Tell me about yourself.
key_points: short present-past-future structure, under two minutes
education and relevant skills
one or two concrete projects or achievements with results
why this role / company fits, no personal life story

question: Walk me through the project you are most proud of.
key_points: the problem and why it mattered
your own role and the technical choices you made
a measurable result or number
a challenge you hit and what you learnt

question: What is your biggest weakness?
key_points: a real, relevant weakness, not a disguised strength
a specific example of it
concrete steps taken to improve
evidence of progress

question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate. What did you do?
key_points: uses a specific situation (STAR: situation, task, action, result)
listened to the other view and stayed respectful
used data or discussion to resolve it
outcome and what was learnt

question: Why should we hire you?
key_points: links own skills to the role's needs
backs claims with evidence such as projects, internships or results
shows eagerness to learn and team fit
concise and confident, not arrogant
